title: Government reconsiders overhaul of working holiday visa scheme
transcript:
Speaker 0: Well, farmers are hopeful that the federal government will compromise on changes to backpacker visas,
Speaker 0: which they warn, could create labor shortages and threaten food security.
Speaker 0: Media reports have suggested the government will back down on proposed caps for working holiday makers
Speaker 0: and extend requirements
Speaker 0: to stay in rural areas.
Speaker 0: Home affairs minister Tony Burke says while the total number of backpackers won't change,
Speaker 0: he's open to some tweaks.
Speaker 1: The ideal landing place, if I can put it in those terms is this. We get the net overseas migration outcome that I need and Australia needs.
Speaker 1: And we do it in a way that industry gets the workforce that it needs.
Speaker 0: That's the home affairs minister, Tony Burke speaking on Friday. Well, Michael Gerran is CEO of the National Farmers Federation
Speaker 0: and joins me now. Hi, Michael. Welcome to the program.
Speaker 0: Yes. Good morning to you. What are you hearing from government on where these changes are at? Are are you hopeful?
Speaker 2: We are hopeful. This has had an enormous emotional toll on producers across Australia. One in seven
Speaker 2: of our workers on farms come on some form of backpacker visa, and to have that unilaterally slowed up in the middle of the year created enormous angst across
Speaker 2: many communities and family farming businesses.
Speaker 2: That said, the Government and the National Farmers Federation have been in deep negotiations for a number of weeks now. We acknowledge the minister for sitting down with us and working with the issues.
Speaker 2: In good faith, we've agreed not to talk to the detail of that until the negotiations are finished, we remain there, we remain making progress, and the conversations are in good faith. So we're very hopeful
Speaker 2: that in the not too distant future we'll have some announcements from the minister that recognizes
Speaker 2: the needs of agriculture,
Speaker 2: the needs of food security in Australia,
Speaker 0: and can put at rest the deep concerns that many producers currently have. So what were the concerns that were most worrying for the sector about what the government has been proposing?
Speaker 2: Well, we simply wouldn't have the workers we need to plant crops and to harvest crops. As I said before, one in seven workers
Speaker 2: these days and for quite some time, in Australia have been some form of backpackers or overseas workers.
Speaker 2: People who come to Australia,
Speaker 2: enjoy Australia,
Speaker 2: do a bit of work, spend the money while they're here, and head home as advocates for Australia.
Speaker 2: At exactly the same time, can I say that a lot of our young people that might end up farming overseas, learning about different cultures
Speaker 2: in the globe before settling down to their work? So,
Speaker 2: you know, to have that at risk, at real risk, to have
Speaker 2: producers not able to be confident that they would get their workers in the way they have for years, in terms of them applying for the visas, getting their visas quickly and getting into country. Having that put all at risk at harvest this year was of deep concern
Speaker 2: and,
Speaker 2: know, as I said, it had an enormous emotional toll on many communities and many farmers.
Speaker 2: But again, we're now in those deep negotiations for several weeks, and we're really hopeful that we can find a place that recognizes the absolute needs of regional communities and agriculture.
Speaker 0: The government had been proposing the introduction of a ballot system for non British backpackers seeking to extend
Speaker 0: their stay. What were the particular concerns around that proposal?
Speaker 2: Yes. So ballots mean they have no confidence they can come back for a second or third year. It's essentially a lottery.
Speaker 2: And there are many examples of where that doesn't work. One being that young people often travel in two or threes
Speaker 2: for a bit of protection and safety in the same way as we like our children traveling with friends when they go overseas.
Speaker 2: So to go into a ballot and not know whether all three of you will get the ballot, one might and two might not, so therefore the third one probably won't come, it creates all sorts of confusion, ambiguity,
Speaker 2: and no confidence that they can get that second year ballot. So the ballot system is proposed
Speaker 2: with a cap of, I think, 5% in year three. It simply won't work for agriculture,
Speaker 2: simply won't work because we have people that don't have confidence
Speaker 2: in the second and third year billets, therefore won't come for the first year. People that come for the first year and get trained then can't come back when they're at the most productive.
Speaker 2: It's an element of what was proposed that won't work and is part of the negotiations we're currently having with the minister.
Speaker 0: Tell me about the effect of the the slowdown of processing of holiday maker visas.
Speaker 0: What do you... What have you been seeing with that?
Speaker 2: It's been very, very difficult. So we've seen some vegetables left in the ground in the worst case scenario.
Speaker 2: We've
Speaker 2: Australians, if I can say, come out of retirement to drive ahead. It's been incredibly difficult. It has had an enormous emotional toll on communities.
Speaker 2: People have been having to do things that they wouldn't ordinarily do or shouldn't be asked to do. As I said, in the worst case, there's been some real challenges getting some
Speaker 2: short rotation crops like vegetables
Speaker 2: out of the ground. And we're walking into, for example, the cherry season, getting cherries into every supermarket across Australia in time for Christmas. If we don't have confidence that we have access to the workers to pick those cherries,
Speaker 2: then we may not have cherries on the shelves, it being one example. We need confidence. We need a system that works,
Speaker 2: works quickly, everybody knows the rules, overseas people can apply with confidence, get an answer quickly,
Speaker 2: producers can put their workforces together with time on their side,
Speaker 2: and therefore the system works. That's the way it's worked for years. This is not new. It's supported and underpinned Australia and has been a really important part of the social and economic fabric of regional communities and their food system.
Speaker 0: It sounds like things have been progressing in discussions with the government, but should this consultation
Speaker 0: have been done before changes were announced?
Speaker 2: Oh, that's certainly one of the arguments that we have, is that if the minister and the government had sat down with us and talked about their needs around overseas migration
Speaker 2: and allowed us to talk about our needs of agriculture,
Speaker 2: we could very well have avoided this, we could have very well avoided all of the emotional strain and challenges that we've had. It's one of the things we're talking very strongly with the government about, saying we're always open for conversations,
Speaker 2: We're always open to sit down and talk about and understand your needs, put ours beside those, and find a way forward. And in this case,
Speaker 2: to find out that they were slowing up the processing
Speaker 2: as the processing was slowing up, and then being in a rearguard action with all of the implications
Speaker 2: that we've seen since
Speaker 2: could have been avoided, and we hope is one of the lessons we learn and one of the things we can do better going forward.
Speaker 0: Michael Guerin, thank you very much. Thank you.
themes: Backpacker visa policy changes threatening agricultural labor shortages
Food security concerns from proposed working holiday maker restrictions
Government negotiations to modify visa caps and ballot system requirements
